claims.statement: Jon Kleinberg published The Small-World Phenomenon: An Algorithmic Perspective at STOC 2000 pp163–170, and a separate Nature brief Navigation in a Small World 406:845 on 24 August 2000
claims.locator: Cornell original HTML opening/TOC and Nature journal metadata

claims.statement: Kleinberg contrasts existence of short paths with finding them using only local information; critiques uniform random shortcuts for decentralized navigation
claims.locator: STOC abstract and Introduction; Nature abstract

claims.statement: 2D n by n grid has local contacts and long-range choices with probability proportional to lattice distance^-r
Long-range edge likelihood for u-to-v equals d(u,v)^-r divided by sum of weights over candidate vertices
For r=2 with specified p=q=1 2D lattice model a decentralized algorithm achieves expected delivery time O(log² n)
For r=0 any decentralized method incurs Omega(n^(2/3)) expected delivery time in the specified model even though short paths exist
For 0<=r<2 and r>2 any decentralized algorithm has polynomial n lower bounds with model-specific exponents
2D doubled-distance annulus has Theta(d²) vertices; weighted probability scale d^(2-r) is balanced at r=2
claims.locator: STOC after Theorem 3 distance scale argument

claims.statement: In D-dimensional lattice analogue navigability exponent r=D, not universal value two
n denotes linear grid width with n² vertices; log-squared bound is expectation for given model not universal guarantee for human social routing
Milgram experiment's successful short chains and Watts-Strogatz short path model do not by themselves prove decentralized findability
City block Manhattan distance and annulus examples are classroom reconstructions and not historical subject behavior
